Absolute Value: Distance from 0

How do we measure the size of a number without its sign? That measure is the absolute value.

On the number line it is the distance from 0. Positive numbers stay as they are; negative numbers shed their sign. The rules of distance come with it. A length is never negative, and a combined walk never exceeds the sum of its parts. That is the triangle inequality.

For example, 🌡 −3 degrees and +3 degrees are the same distance from 0 degrees. The sign is the direction; the absolute value is the distance.

∣x∣={xx≥0−xx<0|x| = \begin{cases} x & x \ge 0 \\ -x & x < 0 \end{cases}∣x∣={x−x​x≥0x<0​

Examples & Exercises

Prove completely that for all real x,yx, yx,y, the triangle inequality ∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣|x + y| \le |x| + |y|∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣ holds.

∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣|x + y| \le |x| + |y|∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣
Show proof

  1. Both sides are non-negative, so compare their squares. ∣x+y∣2=(x+y)2=x2+2xy+y2|x + y|^2 = (x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2∣x+y∣2=(x+y)2=x2+2xy+y2.

  2. Trap the middle term: xy≤∣xy∣=∣x∣ ∣y∣xy \le |xy| = |x| \, |y|xy≤∣xy∣=∣x∣∣y∣, so ∣x+y∣2≤∣x∣2+2∣x∣ ∣y∣+∣y∣2=(∣x∣+∣y∣)2|x + y|^2 \le |x|^2 + 2|x| \, |y| + |y|^2 = (|x| + |y|)^2∣x+y∣2≤∣x∣2+2∣x∣∣y∣+∣y∣2=(∣x∣+∣y∣)2.

  3. On non-negative numbers the square root preserves order. Taking square roots of both sides gives ∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣|x + y| \le |x| + |y|∣x+y∣≤∣x∣+∣y∣. The proof is complete.

Prove completely that for all real x,yx, yx,y, ∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣≤∣x−y∣\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le |x - y|​∣x∣−∣y∣​≤∣x−y∣ holds.

∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣≤∣x−y∣\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le |x - y|​∣x∣−∣y∣​≤∣x−y∣
Show proof

  1. Since x=(x−y)+yx = (x - y) + yx=(x−y)+y, the triangle inequality gives ∣x∣≤∣x−y∣+∣y∣|x| \le |x - y| + |y|∣x∣≤∣x−y∣+∣y∣. Rearranging, ∣x∣−∣y∣≤∣x−y∣|x| - |y| \le |x - y|∣x∣−∣y∣≤∣x−y∣.

  2. Swapping the roles of xxx and yyy gives ∣y∣−∣x∣≤∣y−x∣|y| - |x| \le |y - x|∣y∣−∣x∣≤∣y−x∣. But ∣y−x∣=∣x−y∣|y - x| = |x - y|∣y−x∣=∣x−y∣, so ∣y∣−∣x∣≤∣x−y∣|y| - |x| \le |x - y|∣y∣−∣x∣≤∣x−y∣ holds too.

  3. Combining the two, ∣∣x∣−∣y∣∣=max⁡(∣x∣−∣y∣,∣y∣−∣x∣)≤∣x−y∣\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| = \max(|x| - |y|, |y| - |x|) \le |x - y|​∣x∣−∣y∣​=max(∣x∣−∣y∣,∣y∣−∣x∣)≤∣x−y∣. The proof is complete.

Find all real xxx satisfying ∣x−1∣<2|x - 1| < 2∣x−1∣<2, and prove the equivalence completely.

∣x−1∣<2  ⟺  −1<x<3|x - 1| < 2 \iff -1 < x < 3∣x−1∣<2⟺−1<x<3
Show proof

  1. By the definition, for r>0r > 0r>0, ∣a∣<r|a| < r∣a∣<r is equivalent to −r<a<r-r < a < r−r<a<r. Check by sign: if a≥0a \ge 0a≥0 then ∣a∣=a|a| = a∣a∣=a, so a<ra < ra<r and −r<0≤a-r < 0 \le a−r<0≤a; if a<0a < 0a<0 then ∣a∣=−a|a| = -a∣a∣=−a, so −a<r-a < r−a<r, i.e. −r<a-r < a−r<a, and a<0<ra < 0 < ra<0<r.

  2. Applying this with a=x−1a = x - 1a=x−1 and r=2r = 2r=2, ∣x−1∣<2|x - 1| < 2∣x−1∣<2 is equivalent to −2<x−1<2-2 < x - 1 < 2−2<x−1<2. Adding 1 throughout gives −1<x<3-1 < x < 3−1<x<3.

  3. So the solution set is the open interval (−1,3)(-1, 3)(−1,3): exactly the points whose distance from 1 is less than 2.
